subject: Pharmacology
topic: Loop vs Thiazide Diuretics Renal Calcium Excretion Mechanisms
stem: A 62-year-old woman with chronic hypertension and osteopenia is evaluated for medication optimization. Her current medications include amlodipine 10 mg daily and hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily. Her 24-hour urinary calcium excretion is measured at 85 mg/day (normal 100-300 mg/day). In contrast, her 66-year-old husband with heart failure is treated with oral furosemide 40 mg daily, and his 24-hour urinary calcium excretion is 380 mg/day. Which of the following transport mechanisms directly explains why thiazide diuretics cause hypocalciuria while loop diuretics promote hypercalciuria?

options.text: Thiazides inhibit the distal convoluted tubule NCCT cotransporter, decreasing intracellular Na+ and stimulating basolateral 3Na+/Ca2+ exchange and passive apical Ca2+ entry, whereas loop diuretics abolish the lumen-positive potential in the thick ascending limb
options.explanation: In the distal convoluted tubule (DCT), THIAZIDE diuretics inhibit the apical Na+-Cl- cotransporter (NCCT). This lowers intracellular sodium concentration, which markedly enhances the electrochemical gradient driving basolateral 3Na+/Ca2+ antiporter (NCX1) activity. Increased NCX1 activity extrudes calcium into the interstitium and lowers intracellular calcium, which accelerates apical calcium reabsorption through TRPV5 calcium channels, producing hypocalciuria and protecting against nephrolithiasis and bone loss. Conversely, LOOP diuretics (furosemide) inhibit the apical Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb. This prevents potassium recycling via apical ROMK channels, collapsing the lumen-positive transepithelial electrical potential (+8 to +10 mV) that normally drives passive paracellular reabsorption of divalent cations (Ca2+ and Mg2+), resulting in hypercalciuria and hypermagnesuria.

options.text: Loop diuretics directly upregulate the apical calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) in the proximal tubule, blocking all calcium reabsorption
options.explanation: CaSR is primarily in the thick ascending limb and parathyroid gland; loop diuretics do not directly bind or activate CaSR.

options.text: Thiazide diuretics stimulate parathyroid hormone release from the parathyroid glands via allosteric activation of adenylate cyclase
options.explanation: Thiazides do not stimulate parathyroid hormone secretion; PTH levels are typically normal or slightly suppressed due to mild hypercalcemia.

options.text: Loop diuretics inhibit mitochondrial carbonic anhydrase in the collecting duct, inducing massive urinary calcium precipitation
options.explanation: Carbonic anhydrase is primarily in the proximal tubule and is inhibited by acetazolamide, not furosemide.

options.text: Thiazide diuretics block the basolateral Ca2+-ATPase pump in medullary collecting duct principal cells
options.explanation: Thiazides act on apical NCCT in the distal convoluted tubule, not on basolateral Ca2+-ATPase in the collecting duct.

subject: Physiology
topic: Aortic Regurgitation Pressure-Volume Loop and Hemodynamic Volume Overload
stem: A 34-year-old woman with a history of bicuspid aortic valve undergoes cardiac catheterization for progressive dyspnea on exertion. Physical examination reveals an early, blowing, decrescendo diastolic murmur heard best at the left third intercostal space with the patient sitting upright and leaning forward in full expiration. Peripheral examination demonstrates bounding 'water-hammer' carotid pulses, head bobbing with each heartbeat (de Musset sign), and a widened pulse pressure (164/52 mm Hg). Echocardiography confirms severe chronic aortic regurgitation with left ventricular eccentric hypertrophy. Which of the following alterations on a left ventricular pressure-volume loop is most characteristic of this patient's chronic compensated valvular lesion compared to a normal heart?

options.text: Marked upward elevation of peak systolic ventricular pressure with unchanged end-diastolic volume and reduced loop width
options.explanation: Upward elevation of peak systolic pressure with preserved or decreased EDV and reduced stroke volume describes isolated severe aortic stenosis, not aortic regurgitation.

options.text: Rightward shift of the end-diastolic volume point with loss of distinct isovolumetric contraction and relaxation phases and massive widening of loop width
options.explanation: Aortic regurgitation (AR) produces a combined VOLUME AND PRESSURE OVERLOAD on the left ventricle. During diastole, blood flows retrograde from the aorta into the left ventricle simultaneously with normal antegrade mitral filling, resulting in a marked increase in end-diastolic volume (EDV shifted far to the right). Because the aortic valve is incompetent and leaks continuously throughout diastole, true isovolumetric contraction and relaxation phases are lost (the pressure-volume loop has rounded vertical boundaries). The regurgitant volume plus effective stroke volume produces a massive increase in total stroke volume (represented by substantial widening of the width of the pressure-volume loop). High stroke volume ejected into the aorta raises peak systolic pressure, while rapid runoff into the LV lowers diastolic pressure, generating a widened pulse pressure.

options.text: Leftward and downward shift of the entire pressure-volume loop with preserved pulse pressure
options.explanation: Leftward and downward shift occurs in hypovolemia or acute blood loss due to reduced preload.

options.text: Parallel rightward displacement of the end-systolic volume point with an acute reduction in left ventricular stroke volume
options.explanation: Pure rightward shift of ESV with reduced stroke volume describes dilated cardiomyopathy with pure systolic failure, not chronic volume-overloaded regurgitation with huge total stroke volume.

options.text: Selective loss of the ventricular ejection phase with immediate isometric filling through the tricuspid valve
options.explanation: The ejection phase is preserved and augmented in aortic regurgitation to accommodate the massive stroke volume.

subject: Microbiology
topic: Diphtheria Toxin and Pseudomonas Exotoxin A EF-2 Inactivation
stem: A 5-year-old unimmunized girl brought from an Eastern European orphanage presents with a 3-day history of low-grade fever, sore throat, and severe cervical lymphadenopathy producing a 'bull neck' appearance. On physical examination, a dense, gray-white, fibrinous pseudomembrane is tightly adherent to her posterior pharyngeal wall and tonsillar pillars; attempting to dislodge the membrane produces brisk bleeding. ECG reveals PR prolongation and first-degree atrioventricular block. The pathogenic organism is an aerobic, non-spore-forming, Gram-positive club-shaped rod containing metachromatic polyphosphate granules on Albert stain. Which of the following molecular mechanisms directly accounts for the cytotoxic cellular lethality of this organism's primary exotoxin?

options.text: ADP-ribosylation of the alpha-inhibitory (Gi) subunit of heterotrimeric G proteins preventing adenylate cyclase inhibition
options.explanation: Gi ADP-ribosylation is the mechanism of pertussis toxin (Bordetella pertussis), which leads to persistent adenylate cyclase activation and lymphocytosis.

options.text: Cleavage of host cell surface membrane ganglioside GM1 receptors by a heat-labile metalloendopeptidase
options.explanation: Vibrio cholerae toxin binds GM1 ganglioside receptors; it does not cleave them.

options.text: Transfer of an ADP-ribose moiety from NAD+ to a diphthamide residue on elongation factor-2 (EF-2), irreversibly halting ribosomal protein synthesis
options.explanation: Corynebacterium diphtheriae produces diphtheria toxin, a potent AB-type exotoxin encoded by the tox gene on a lysogenic beta-corynephage. The B subunit binds the host heparin-binding epidermal growth factor-like precursor on myocardial and neural tissues, mediating receptor-mediated endocytosis. The catalytic A subunit translocates into the cytosol, where it catalyzes the transfer of ADP-ribose from host NAD+ to a modified histidine residue (diphthamide) on ELONGATION FACTOR-2 (EF-2). Inactivation of EF-2 halts ribosome translocation along mRNA, completely arresting cellular protein synthesis. This causes mucosal epithelial necrosis (forming the adherent pseudomembrane), life-threatening toxic myocarditis with arrhythmias and heart block, and demyelinating cranial/peripheral neuropathies. Pseudomonas aeruginosa Exotoxin A utilizes this exact same molecular mechanism (ADP-ribosylation of EF-2).

options.text: Cleavage of the SNARE protein SNAP-25 preventing exocytosis of inhibitory neurotransmitters GABA and glycine
options.explanation: SNAP-25 cleavage is the mechanism of botulinum neurotoxin types A and E, which causes flaccid motor paralysis.

options.text: Lysis of phagolysosomal membranes via a thiol-activated cholesterol-dependent pore-forming cytolysin
options.explanation: Pore formation to escape the phagolysosome is mediated by listeriolysin O in Listeria monocytogenes, not C. diphtheriae.

subject: Genetics
topic: Marfan Syndrome FBN1 Mutations and Microfibril Assembly
stem: A 17-year-old tall, slender adolescent is evaluated following a sports physical. He has long, thin extremities with an arm span-to-height ratio of 1.08. Physical examination reveals arachnodactyly, a positive Steinberg thumb sign, pectus excavatum, severe scoliosis, and bilateral upward and outward (superotemporal) subluxation of the ocular lenses (ectopia lentis). Echocardiography demonstrates marked dilation of the aortic root at the sinuses of Valsalva with mild aortic regurgitation. A younger sibling died suddenly of acute aortic rupture. Which of the following is the underlying molecular defect in this patient's disorder?

options.text: Mutations in the COL5A1 or COL5A2 genes causing defective assembly of type V fibrillar collagen
options.explanation: Classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is caused by type V collagen mutations (COL5A1/COL5A2), presenting with hyperextensible skin, joint hypermobility, and fragile 'cigarette-paper' atrophic scars, without upward ectopia lentis.

options.text: Autosomal dominant mutation in the COL1A1 gene encoding alpha-1 chains of type I collagen
options.explanation: Type I collagen mutations cause Osteogenesis Imperfecta (brittle bones, blue sclerae, hearing loss, dentinogenesis imperfecta), not arachnodactyly or aortic root aneurysm.

options.text: Mutation in the COL3A1 gene causing defective synthesis of type III reticular procollagen
options.explanation: Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome involves type III collagen mutations (COL3A1), causing fragile blood vessels and spontaneous bowel/uterine rupture without marfanoid habitus or ectopia lentis.

options.text: Autosomal dominant mutation in the FBN1 gene encoding fibrillin-1, a glycoprotein that forms the structural microfibrillar scaffold for elastin deposition
options.explanation: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder caused by mutations in the FBN1 gene on chromosome 15q21, which encodes FIBRILLIN-1. Fibrillin-1 is an extracellular matrix glycoprotein that forms microfibrils, which serve as the essential structural scaffold for the deposition of elastin in elastic fibers throughout the aorta, ocular ciliary zonules, and periosteum. Mutated fibrillin-1 weakens the aortic tunica media (cystic medial necrosis), predisposing to aortic root aneurysm and dissection. Furthermore, microfibrils normally sequester latent transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta); defective fibrillin-1 leads to excessive free TGF-beta signaling, promoting matrix metalloproteinase-mediated elastic fiber destruction and skeletal elongation. Upward/outward ectopia lentis is pathognomonic (in contrast to downward/inward subluxation in homocystinuria).

options.text: Deficiency of lysyl hydroxylase causing impaired covalent intermolecular cross-linking of collagen fibrils
options.explanation: Kyphoscoliotic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is caused by lysyl hydroxylase deficiency, presenting with severe progressive scoliosis and ocular fragility, without fibrillin-1 involvement.

subject: Biochemistry
topic: Classic Galactosemia vs Galactokinase Deficiency Biochemical Spectrum
stem: A 3-week-old female infant is brought to the emergency department for severe lethargy, vomiting, and yellow discoloration of the skin and eyes that began shortly after breastfeeding was initiated. Physical examination reveals an irritable, deeply jaundiced infant with hepatosplenomegaly, full fontanelle, and bilateral dense nuclear cataracts. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates: total bilirubin 14.2 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 8.8 mg/dL, AST 340 U/L, ALT 290 U/L, and prolonged prothrombin time (INR 2.4). Blood cultures grow Escherichia coli. Urinalysis reveals positive non-glucose reducing substances with a negative glucose dipstick. Which of the following enzymatic deficiencies is responsible for this infant's multi-organ failure and cataracts?

options.text: Galactokinase (GALK) deficiency causing isolated benign cataracts without systemic organ toxicity
options.explanation: Galactokinase deficiency causes isolated cataract formation from galactitol accumulation without hepatomegaly, jaundice, liver dysfunction, or E. coli sepsis.

options.text: UDP-galactose 4-epimerase (GALE) deficiency restricted solely to peripheral mature erythrocytes
options.explanation: GALE deficiency can cause a mild peripheral form or severe classic-like disease, but the classic presentation with E. coli sepsis and early neonatal hepatic collapse is GALT deficiency.

options.text: Aldolase B (fructose-1-phosphate aldolase) deficiency causing toxic fructose-1-phosphate accumulation
options.explanation: Hereditary fructose intolerance (aldolase B deficiency) causes hypoglycemia, vomiting, and hepatomegaly upon introduction of fructose/sucrose (fruits, juice), not during breastfeeding (lactose).

options.text: Fructokinase deficiency causing benign, asymptomatic presence of reducing sugars in the urine
options.explanation: Essential fructosuria (fructokinase deficiency) is a completely benign, asymptomatic condition detected incidentally by non-glucose reducing sugars in urine.

options.text: Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT) deficiency causing toxic intracellular accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate and galactitol
options.explanation: CLASSIC GALACTOSEMIA is an autosomal recessive inborn error of carbohydrate metabolism caused by deficiency of GALACTOSE-1-PHOSPHATE URIDYLTRANSFERASE (GALT). GALT converts galactose-1-phosphate and UDP-glucose into glucose-1-phosphate and UDP-galactose. In GALT deficiency, toxic galactose-1-phosphate accumulates inside hepatocytes, renal tubular cells, and neurons, depleting inorganic phosphate and halting cellular ATP generation. This causes severe hepatomegaly, cirrhosis, renal Fanconi syndrome, intellectual disability, and profound susceptibility to systemic Escherichia coli sepsis. Concurrently, excess circulating galactose is shunted via ALDOSE REDUCTASE into GALACTITOL, which accumulates inside lens fibers, creating an osmotic gradient that draws water into the lens and causes cataracts. In contrast, GALACTOKINASE (GALK) deficiency causes ONLY benign cataracts from galactitol without liver failure or E. coli sepsis.

subject: Immunology
topic: Chronic Granulomatous Disease gp91phox and Respiratory Burst Failure
stem: A 3-year-old boy is hospitalized for the fourth time with invasive bacterial and fungal infections, including Serratia marcescens osteomyelitis, a liver abscess requiring surgical drainage that grew Staphylococcus aureus, and recurrent Aspergillus fumigatus pneumonia. Physical examination reveals cervical lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. Dihydrorhodamine 123 (DHR) flow cytometry demonstrates a complete absence of green fluorescence upon phorbol myristate acetate stimulation of neutrophils. Nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) slide test shows failure of neutrophils to reduce yellow NBT dye to blue formazan precipitate. Which of the following enzymatic complexes is defective in this patient?

options.text: Neutrophil membrane-bound NADPH oxidase (phox) complex preventing generation of superoxide radicals (O2•-)
options.explanation: Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) is an inherited immunodeficiency most commonly caused by an X-linked recessive mutation in the CYBB gene encoding the gp91phox subunit of the NADPH oxidase complex. NADPH oxidase normally transfers electrons from cytosolic NADPH to molecular oxygen, generating SUPEROXIDE ANIONS (O2•-), the essential precursor for hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), hydroxyl radicals (•OH), and hypochlorous acid (HOCl via myeloperoxidase). Without NADPH oxidase, phagocytes cannot generate the respiratory burst required to kill catalase-positive organisms (Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas/Burkholderia cepacia, Serratia marcescens, Nocardia, Aspergillus). Catalase-positive pathogens degrade their own endogenous H2O2, depriving the neutrophil of any substrate for myeloperoxidase killing, resulting in recurrent abscesses, granuloma formation, and negative DHR/NBT tests.

options.text: Lysosomal myeloperoxidase (MPO) in primary azurophilic granules preventing conversion of H2O2 to hypochlorous acid
options.explanation: MPO deficiency causes impaired HOCl production, but neutrophils generate normal superoxide and H2O2, producing a normal DHR flow cytometry and NBT reduction.

options.text: Leukocyte beta-2 integrin CD18 subunit preventing firm endothelial adhesion and extravasation
options.explanation: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 (LAD-1) is caused by CD18/LFA-1 deficiency, presenting with delayed umbilical cord separation, recurrent infections WITHOUT pus, and marked leukocytosis.

options.text: Cytosolic glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase causing complete depletion of erythroid NADPH stores
options.explanation: G6PD deficiency causes hemolytic anemia, not isolated recurrent invasive staphylococcal and fungal granulomatous abscesses.

options.text: Vesicular trafficking regulator protein (LYST) preventing phagolysosomal fusion in granulocytes
options.explanation: LYST mutations cause Chédiak-Higashi syndrome, characterized by partial albinism, peripheral neuropathy, and giant lysosomal granules in granulocytes.

subject: Pathology
topic: Chronic Myeloid Leukemia BCR-ABL1 Translocation and Constitutive Tyrosine Kinase
stem: A 54-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue, early satiety, and left upper quadrant fullness. Physical examination reveals massive splenomegaly extending 8 cm below the left costal margin without lymphadenopathy. Complete blood count shows: WBC 142,000/microL with a full spectrum of granulocytic precursors (myelocytes, metamyelocytes, band forms), absolute basophilia (4%), absolute eosinophilia, hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, and platelets 580,000/microL. Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score is markedly decreased at 12 (normal 40-130). Bone marrow cytogenetics confirms a reciprocal translocation t(9;22)(q34;q11). Which of the following molecular mechanisms directly drives the unrestrained granulocytic proliferation in this disease?

options.text: Constitutive point mutation in the pseudokinase domain of JAK2 (V617F) causing hypersensitivity to erythropoietin
options.explanation: JAK2 V617F is the hallmark of polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, and primary myelofibrosis, not chronic myeloid leukemia.

options.text: Fusion of the BCR and ABL1 genes generating a chimeric protein with constitutive, ligand-independent tyrosine kinase activity
options.explanation: Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm defined by the Philadelphia chromosome, a reciprocal translocation t(9;22)(q34;q11). This translocates the ABL1 proto-oncogene from chromosome 9 to the BCR gene on chromosome 22, creating a chimeric BCR-ABL1 fusion gene. The resulting BCR-ABL1 fusion protein (p210 or p190) functions as a CONSTITUTIVELY ACTIVE NON-RECEPTOR TYROSINE KINASE that autophosphorylates and activates downstream oncogenic pathways (RAS/MAPK, JAK/STAT, PI3K/Akt). This drives uncontrolled granulocyte proliferation, inhibits apoptosis, and reduces cell adhesion to bone marrow stroma. CML is distinguished from a reactive leukemoid reaction by a LOW leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score, absolute basophilia, and presence of the t(9;22) translocation.

options.text: Translocation t(15;17)(q22;q21) creating a PML-RARA fusion protein that blocks promyelocytic differentiation
options.explanation: PML-RARA is the hallmark of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL, AML M3), presenting with severe coagulopathy/DIC, not indolent massive granulocytosis.

options.text: Translocation t(8;14)(q24;q32) juxtaposing the c-MYC oncogene with the immunoglobulin heavy-chain promoter
options.explanation: c-MYC translocation t(8;14) drives Burkitt lymphoma, an aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma with starry-sky histology.

options.text: Overexpression of the anti-apoptotic protein BCL-2 via translocation t(14;18)(q32;q21)
options.explanation: t(14;18) translocation causes follicular lymphoma by upregulating BCL-2, preventing apoptosis in germinal center B cells.

subject: Medicine
topic: Primary vs Secondary Adrenal Insufficiency and Aldosterone Preservation
stem: A 36-year-old woman presents with severe fatigue, weight loss, dizziness on standing, and salt craving. Physical examination reveals orthostatic hypotension (blood pressure drops from 108/68 mm Hg supine to 84/52 mm Hg standing) and generalized bronze hyperpigmentation, particularly prominent on the palmar creases, vermilion border of the lips, and recent surgical scars. Serum electrolytes reveal: sodium 128 mEq/L, potassium 5.6 mEq/L, chloride 96 mEq/L, and bicarbonate 20 mEq/L. Serum morning cortisol is 2.4 mcg/dL (normal 5-25 mcg/dL). Administration of synthetic ACTH (cosyntropin 250 mcg IV) produces a 60-minute serum cortisol of 2.8 mcg/dL. Plasma ACTH is markedly elevated at 480 pg/mL (normal 10-60 pg/mL). Which of the following physiological principles explains why aldosterone secretion is severely deficient in primary adrenal insufficiency but preserved in secondary adrenal insufficiency?

options.text: Pituitary ACTH directly stimulates the apical 21-hydroxylase enzyme in the zona glomerulosa, which is spared in secondary failure
options.explanation: ACTH does not selectively stimulate 21-hydroxylase; aldosterone regulation is independent of pituitary ACTH and is governed by angiotensin II.

options.text: Cortisol is converted into aldosterone within the hepatic portal circulation via the 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase enzyme
options.explanation: Cortisol is not converted into aldosterone; 11-beta-HSD type 2 converts cortisol to inactive cortisone in the kidney to prevent mineralocorticoid receptor overactivation.

options.text: Aldosterone secretion from the zona glomerulosa is primarily regulated by the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and potassium, not by pituitary ACTH
options.explanation: In PRIMARY adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), autoimmune destruction or infiltrative disease destroys all three layers of the adrenal cortex (zona glomerulosa, fasciculata, and reticularis). Loss of the zona glomerulosa eliminates ALDOSTERONE, causing salt wasting, severe hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypovolemia, and orthostatic hypotension. Furthermore, loss of cortisol removes negative feedback on the pituitary, causing massive ACTH and pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) secretion; cleavage of POMC generates alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH), which binds melanocortin-1 receptors (MC1R) on epidermal melanocytes to produce hyperpigmentation. In contrast, in SECONDARY adrenal insufficiency (pituitary ACTH deficiency) or tertiary insufficiency (hypothalamic CRH deficiency), the adrenal cortex is intact. Because aldosterone secretion is physiologically controlled by the RENIN-ANGIOTENSIN SYSTEM (angiotensin II) and serum POTASSIUM, aldosterone secretion is PRESERVED, preventing severe hyperkalemia, volume collapse, or cutaneous hyperpigmentation.

options.text: Secondary adrenal insufficiency involves compensatory hypersecretion of hypothalamic vasopressin that stimulates V1a aldosterone receptors
options.explanation: Vasopressin does not maintain normal aldosterone secretion in secondary adrenal insufficiency; the intact renin-angiotensin axis maintains it.

options.text: The zona glomerulosa undergoes selective hyperplastic hypertrophy in response to deficient hypothalamic corticotropin-releasing hormone
options.explanation: The zona glomerulosa does not hypertrophy in secondary adrenal insufficiency; it simply functions normally under independent renin-angiotensin control.

subject: Neurology
topic: Syringomyelia Anterior White Commissure Spinothalamic Decussation
stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with bilateral burns on her fingertips and forearms that occurred while cooking; she states she felt no pain or heat when touching hot cookware. Neurological examination reveals complete loss of pain and temperature sensation across both shoulders, arms, and upper chest in a 'cape-like' distribution, with intact light touch, vibration sense, and proprioception in the exact same dermatomal regions. Muscle strength and deep tendon reflexes are initially preserved in all four extremities. Sagittal T1-weighted cervical spine MRI demonstrates a cystic fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) within the central cord extending from C3 to T2, associated with tonsillar ectopia 6 mm below the foramen magnum (Chiari I malformation). Which of the following neuroanatomical structures was damaged first by the expanding central fluid cavity to produce this dissociated sensory loss?

options.text: Posterior columns (fasciculus cuneatus and gracilis) carrying primary ascending mechanoreceptor axons
options.explanation: Damage to the posterior columns causes loss of vibration, conscious proprioception, and fine touch, not selective loss of pain and temperature.

options.text: Lateral corticospinal tract carrying descending upper motor neuron efferents from the motor cortex
options.explanation: Lateral corticospinal tract compression causes spastic paraparesis and hyperreflexia below the lesion, not dermatomal cape-like analgesia.

options.text: Substantia gelatinosa of the dorsal root entry zone bilaterally throughout all sacral segments
options.explanation: Syringomyelia typically affects the cervical cord, not sacral segments; it initially damages crossing commissural fibers rather than dorsal root entry zones.

options.text: Anterior white commissure carrying crossing second-order spinothalamic axons
options.explanation: Syringomyelia is a chronic cystic cavitary expansion of the central canal of the spinal cord (syrinx), most frequently located in the cervical cord and strongly associated with Chiari I malformations. As the central fluid cavity expands, it first compresses and disrupts the ANTERIOR WHITE COMMISSURE. The anterior white commissure contains the second-order axons of the anterolateral (spinothalamic) system that decussate immediately after synapsing in the dorsal horn (substantia gelatinosa). Disruption of these crossing fibers abolishes bilateral pain and temperature sensation in the affected dermatomes ('cape-like' distribution). The posterior columns (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus), which ascend ipsilaterally without crossing in the spinal cord, are spared initially, producing the classic DISSOCIATED SENSORY LOSS (loss of pain/temperature with preserved light touch, vibration, and proprioception). As the syrinx enlarges further, it can compress anterior horn lower motor neurons (causing flaccid arm weakness and muscle wasting) and lateral corticospinal tracts (spastic leg weakness).

options.text: Spinoreticular tracts in the ventrolateral funiculus mediating autonomic cardiovascular reflexes
options.explanation: Spinoreticular damage does not explain the selective, bilateral cape-like sensory dissociation of pain and temperature.

subject: Physiology
topic: High-Altitude Acclimatization and 2,3-BPG Right Shift
stem: A 29-year-old mountaineer ascends rapidly from sea level to a base camp at 14,500 feet (4,420 meters), where atmospheric pressure is approximately 440 mm Hg. Within 24 hours, he experiences mild headache, fatigue, and dyspnea on exertion. Arterial blood gas on ambient air reveals: pH 7.48, PaCO2 28 mm Hg, PaO2 44 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 21 mEq/L. Over the next 5 days of gradual acclimatization, his resting ventilation remains elevated, and his erythrocyte 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) concentration increases by 45%. Which of the following alterations in oxygen transport and acid-base homeostasis occurs as a consequence of this 5-day physiological acclimatization?

options.text: Leftward shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve driven by massive downregulation of 2,3-BPG
options.explanation: Hypoxia and alkalosis stimulate 2,3-BPG production; 2,3-BPG increases (not decreases) and shifts the curve to the right, facilitating tissue oxygen release.

options.text: Renal retention of hydrogen ions and bicarbonate causing a secondary high anion gap metabolic alkalosis
options.explanation: The kidneys excrete bicarbonate (causing compensatory non-gap metabolic acidosis) to counteract respiratory alkalosis, not retain it.

options.text: Complete suppression of erythropoietin secretion by renal juxtaglomerular apparatus due to hypocapnic vasoconstriction
options.explanation: Erythropoietin is secreted by peritubular interstitial cells in response to tissue hypoxia (HIF-1alpha); EPO is markedly upregulated, increasing red cell mass.

options.text: Permanent closure of the peripheral chemoreceptor potassium channels preventing any further ventilatory response
options.explanation: Peripheral chemoreceptors remain active and sensitized during acclimatization, maintaining hyperventilation.

options.text: Rightward shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve facilitating peripheral oxygen unloading, accompanied by renal bicarbonate excretion to normalize arterial pH
options.explanation: At high altitude, low barometric pressure reduces inspired PO2 (PiO2 = 0.21 x (440 - 47) = 82 mm Hg), causing arterial hypoxemia. Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid bodies) trigger hyperventilation, blowing off CO2 and inducing acute respiratory alkalosis (high pH, low PaCO2). Over several days, physiological ACCLIMATIZATION occurs: (1) Severe hypoxemia stimulates erythrocyte glycolysis, increasing production of 2,3-BISPHOSPHOGLYCERATE (2,3-BPG) via the Rapoport-Luebering shunt. 2,3-BPG binds the central cavity of the deoxyhemoglobin tetramer, stabilizing the T (taut) state and shifting the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the RIGHT (increasing P50), which facilitates peripheral tissue oxygen unloading despite arterial hypoxemia. (2) The kidneys compensate for respiratory alkalosis by downregulating proximal bicarbonate reabsorption and excreting bicarbonate in the urine, restoring arterial pH toward normal (compensatory metabolic acidosis). (3) Renal interstitial peritubular cells sense hypoxia and secrete ERYTHROPOIETIN (EPO), increasing hematocrit and blood oxygen-carrying capacity.

subject: Pharmacology
topic: Succinylcholine Phase I vs Phase II Block and Butyrylcholinesterase
stem: A 34-year-old man undergoes rapid sequence intubation for an emergent appendectomy. Anesthesia is induced with intravenous propofol followed by intravenous succinylcholine 1.5 mg/kg. Muscle fasciculations are noted in his face and extremities followed by complete flaccidity. Two hours after the conclusion of the 30-minute procedure, the patient remains paralyzed and apneic, requiring continued mechanical ventilation. Train-of-four (TOF) peripheral nerve stimulation reveals a sustained, equal reduction in twitch amplitude across all four twitches without fade (equal four twitches of diminished height). Post-tetanic potentiation is absent. Administration of intravenous neostigmine at this time produces a further deepening of neuromuscular blockade. Which of the following genetic or enzymatic abnormalities explains this patient's prolonged paralysis?

options.text: Genetic deficiency of plasma butyrylcholinesterase (pseudocholinesterase) prolonging Phase I depolarization blockade
options.explanation: Succinylcholine is a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker consisting of two linked acetylcholine molecules. It binds postsynaptic nicotinic receptors at the motor endplate, inducing persistent opening of Na+ channels and generating initial muscle fasciculations followed by flaccid paralysis (PHASE I BLOCK). Phase I block is characterized on train-of-four (TOF) stimulation by CONSTANT, EQUAL TWITCH HEIGHT (NO FADE) and ABSENCE of post-tetanic potentiation. Importantly, administration of an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (neostigmine) during Phase I worsens the block by increasing synaptic ACh concentration, intensifying depolarization. Succinylcholine is rapidly hydrolyzed in the bloodstream by PLASMA BUTYRYLCHOLINESTERASE (pseudocholinesterase), with a normal duration of 5-10 minutes. Patients with atypical or deficient butyrylcholinesterase (e.g., homozygous atypical BCHE gene variant) cannot metabolize succinylcholine, leading to persistent, massive Phase I depolarization blockade and prolonged apnea lasting several hours.

options.text: Homozygous deletion of the cardiac sodium-calcium exchanger (NCX1) in the myoplasm
options.explanation: NCX1 is cardiac-specific; it does not metabolize neuromuscular blockers or regulate skeletal neuromuscular transmission.

options.text: Constitutive overactivation of synaptic acetylcholinesterase in the neuromuscular junction
options.explanation: Overactive acetylcholinesterase would accelerate acetylcholine degradation, shortening (not prolonging) neuromuscular transmission.

options.text: Autoantibodies directed against presynaptic choline acetyltransferase halting acetylcholine synthesis
options.explanation: Autoantibodies to choline acetyltransferase do not occur in acute succinylcholine-induced prolonged apnea.

options.text: Acquired deficiency of skeletal muscle dystrophin resulting in generalized endplate receptor internalization
options.explanation: Dystrophin deficiency causes muscular dystrophy; it does not impair plasma pseudocholinesterase-mediated drug clearance.

subject: Physiology
topic: Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome Secretin Paradoxical Gastrin Stimulation
stem: A 42-year-old man presents with severe, recurrent burning epigastric pain, watery diarrhea, and weight loss. Upper endoscopy reveals multiple deep ulcerations in the duodenal bulb and jejunum, accompanied by prominent gastric rugal fold hypertrophy. Fasting serum gastrin concentration is markedly elevated at 1,450 pg/mL (normal < 100 pg/mL), and gastric pH is 1.4. To definitively differentiate a gastrinoma from non-neoplastic hypergastrinemia, an intravenous secretin stimulation test is performed. Which of the following hormonal responses to secretin administration confirms the diagnosis of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome?

options.text: Immediate precipitous drop in serum gastrin to undetectable levels within 15 minutes
options.explanation: A drop in serum gastrin in response to secretin is the normal physiological response observed in non-neoplastic hypergastrinemia (e.g., G-cell hyperplasia or proton pump inhibitor use).

options.text: Paradoxical elevation in serum gastrin concentration exceeding 120 pg/mL above baseline
options.explanation: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (ZES) is caused by a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor (gastrinoma), typically located in the duodenum or pancreas ('gastrinoma triangle'). Hypergastrinemia stimulates gastric parietal cells via CCK-B receptors to hypersecrete hydrochloric acid, causing refractory, recurrent peptic ulcers (often post-bulbar or in the jejunum) and prominent gastric mucosal hypertrophy. The gold-standard confirmatory test is the INTRAVENOUS SECRETIN STIMULATION TEST. In normal physiological states, secretin (released by duodenal S cells in response to luminal acid) INHIBITS normal antral G-cell gastrin release. In contrast, in patients with gastrinomas, secretin PARADOXICALLY STIMULATES gastrinoma cells via secretin receptors, causing a rapid and marked rise in serum gastrin (increase >= 120 pg/mL above baseline within 2 to 30 minutes), definitively establishing the diagnosis.

options.text: Selective suppression of gastric intrinsic factor secretion with profound elevation of somatostatin
options.explanation: Secretin does not selectively block intrinsic factor; its diagnostic utility rests entirely on paradoxical gastrin release from neoplastic gastrinoma cells.

options.text: Massive stimulation of duodenal cholecystokinin secretion triggering biliary colic
options.explanation: Secretin stimulates pancreatic ductal bicarbonate secretion and biliary bicarbonate flow, but CCK hypersecretion is not a diagnostic marker for ZES.

options.text: Paradoxical alkalinization of gastric secretions to pH > 7.0 due to parietal cell exhaustion
options.explanation: Parietal cells remain hyperstimulated by the massive gastrin surge, maintaining severe gastric hyperacidity (pH < 2.0).

subject: Biochemistry
topic: Maple Syrup Urine Disease Branched-Chain Alpha-Ketoacid Dehydrogenase
stem: A 6-day-old male infant born to consanguineous parents develops poor feeding, progressive lethargy, and vomiting. On physical examination, he is stuporous with alternating episodes of hypertonia and hypotonia, and characteristic dystonic cycling movements of his extremities ('fencing and bicycling'). His diapers emit a sweet, caramelized maple syrup-like odor. Serum amino acid quantification demonstrates massive elevation of leucine, isoleucine, and valine, with detection of alloisoleucine. Arterial blood gas reveals severe metabolic acidosis without hyperammonemia. Which of the following cofactors is essential for the enzymatic complex whose deficiency produces this infant's condition?

options.text: Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) and molecular oxygen
options.explanation: BH4 is the cofactor for aromatic amino acid hydroxylases (phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan hydroxylase) and nitric oxide synthase; deficiency causes hyperphenylalaninemia, not MSUD.

options.text: Pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) and heme
options.explanation: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) is the cofactor for transaminases and cystathionine beta-synthase; defect causes homocystinuria, not BCAA accumulation.

options.text: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), lipoic acid, coenzyme A, FAD, and NAD+ (Tender Loving Care For Nancy)
options.explanation: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) is an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism caused by deficiency of the mitochondrial BRANCHED-CHAIN ALPHA-KETO ACID DEHYDROGENASE (BCKDH) complex. BCKDH catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-ketoacids derived from the branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs): LEUCINE, ISOLEUCINE, and VALINE (mnemonic: 'I Love Vermont maple syrup'). The BCKDH complex is analogous in structure and mechanism to the pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complexes, requiring the exact same FIVE COFACTORS: (1) Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP, vitamin B1), (2) Lipoic acid, (3) Coenzyme A (pantothenic acid, B5), (4) FAD (riboflavin, B2), and (5) NAD+ (niacin, B3). Accumulation of leucine and its ketoacid (alpha-ketoisocaproate) is neurotoxic, causing cerebral edema, encephalopathy, and dystonia. A subset of patients with thiamine-responsive MSUD improve with high-dose thiamine supplementation.

options.text: Adenosylcobalamin (vitamin B12) and biotin (vitamin B7)
options.explanation: Adenosylcobalamin is the cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, and biotin is for carboxylases (propionyl-CoA carboxylase, pyruvate carboxylase).

options.text: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) and copper
options.explanation: Ascorbic acid and copper are cofactors for dopamine beta-hydroxylase and lysyl oxidase (collagen cross-linking), not alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenases.

subject: Microbiology
topic: Streptococcus pneumoniae Capsule and Bacterial Transformation
stem: In a laboratory experiment replicating the classic Avery-MacLeod-McCarty and Griffith experiments, mice are injected subcutaneously with living, unencapsulated, non-virulent 'rough' (R) strain Streptococcus pneumoniae and survive without disease. A second group of mice is injected with heat-killed, encapsulated, virulent 'smooth' (S) strain S. pneumoniae and also survives. However, when mice are injected with a mixture of living rough (R) strain bacteria AND heat-killed smooth (S) strain bacteria, the mice die of fulminant pneumococcal bacteremia, and living encapsulated smooth (S) strain pneumococci are recovered from their cardiac blood. Which of the following genetic processes explains the emergence of the virulent encapsulated bacteria in this experiment?

options.text: Generalized transduction mediated by a lytic bacteriophage packaging random host chromosomal fragments
options.explanation: Transduction requires an intermediate bacteriophage virus to transfer genetic material; Griffith's experiment used cell-free heat-killed extracts without phage involvement.

options.text: F-plasmid-mediated conjugative transfer of an autonomous episome through a specialized sex pilus
options.explanation: Conjugation requires direct cell-to-cell contact between viable donor and recipient bacteria via a sex pilus; heat-killed bacteria cannot conjugate.

options.text: Site-specific lysogenic conversion mediated by a temperate bacteriophage integrating a prophage genome
options.explanation: Lysogenic conversion occurs in Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Streptococcus pyogenes (erythrogenic toxin), and Clostridium botulinum, not pneumococcal transformation.

options.text: Natural bacterial transformation via uptake and homologous recombination of naked extracellular DNA fragments from the heat-killed donor strain
options.explanation: Bacterial TRANSFORMATION is the process by which naturally competent bacteria bind, import, and incorporate exogenous 'naked' environmental DNA fragments into their own chromosome through homologous recombination. Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Neisseria species are the classical 'SHiN' bacteria that exhibit natural competence. In the Griffith and Avery experiments, heat-killed smooth (S) strain pneumococci lysed, releasing naked double-stranded DNA fragments containing the functional capsular polysaccharide gene. Living rough (R) strain bacteria expressed cell-wall competence factors (Com proteins), took up the naked capsular gene, incorporated it into their genome, and synthesized the antiphagocytic polysaccharide capsule, rendering them virulent.

options.text: Transposition of a mobile genetic insertion sequence mediated by transposase jumping between non-homologous plasmids
options.explanation: Transposons jump within or between DNA molecules in living cells; transformation specifically refers to the uptake of free extracellular environmental DNA.

topic: Minimal Change Disease Loss of Glomerular Polyanion Charge Barrier
stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician due to sudden puffiness around his eyes that is most prominent in the morning, along with abdominal distension and swollen feet. Blood pressure is normal at 96/60 mm Hg. Physical examination reveals periorbital edema, shifting dullness on abdominal percussion, and 2+ pitting pretibial edema. Urinalysis demonstrates 4+ protein with zero erythrocytes or red blood cell casts. Twenty-four-hour urine protein quantification reveals 4.2 g/day of protein, of which > 90% is albumin (highly selective proteinuria). Serum albumin is 1.8 g/dL and total cholesterol is 340 mg/dL. Renal biopsy shows completely normal glomerular architecture on light microscopy and negative immunofluorescence. Transmission electron microscopy demonstrates diffuse, uniform effacement of visceral epithelial cell foot processes (podocytes). Which of the following pathophysiological alterations directly accounts for the highly selective albuminuria in this patient?

options.text: Subepithelial immune complex deposition causing mechanical rupture of the lamina densa and podocyte apoptosis
options.explanation: Subepithelial immune complex deposition (with spike-and-dome appearance) occurs in membranous nephropathy, causing non-selective proteinuria.

options.text: Subendothelial immune complex deposition with mesangial interposition and duplication of the basement membrane
options.explanation: Subendothelial deposits with 'tram-track' basement membrane splitting occur in membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN), causing nephritic/nephrotic syndrome.

options.text: Widespread mesangial expansion and formation of periodic acid-Schiff-positive nodular glomerulosclerosis lesions
options.explanation: Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodular glomerulosclerosis is the hallmark of diabetic nephropathy, not pediatric minimal change disease.

options.text: Anti-GBM IgG autoantibodies binding non-collagenous domain 1 of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen
options.explanation: Anti-GBM antibodies cause Goodpasture disease, presenting with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, alveolar hemorrhage, and linear IgG on immunofluorescence.

options.text: Cytokine-mediated loss of negatively charged heparan sulfate and sialoglycoproteins on the glomerular basement membrane and podocyte glycocalyx
options.explanation: Minimal change disease (MCD) is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children. It is mediated by T-cell dysfunction leading to release of circulating permeability factors (such as IL-13 and hemopexin). The glomerular filtration barrier consists of three layers: fenestrated capillary endothelium, glomerular basement membrane (GBM), and visceral epithelial foot processes (podocytes) with slit diaphragms. The GBM and podocyte glycocalyx are richly coated with NEGATIVELY CHARGED POLYANIONS, primarily HEPARAN SULFATE proteoglycans and sialoglycoproteins. Because serum albumin is also negatively charged at physiological pH, it is electrostatically repelled by the normal intact charge barrier. In MCD, immune cytokines neutralize or degrade the negative charge barrier, permitting albumin (radius 3.6 nm) to cross the filtration barrier unimpeded, resulting in HIGHLY SELECTIVE PROTEINURIA (albuminuria without larger globulins). Effacement of foot processes is a secondary response to podocyte cytoskeletal stress.

subject: Physiology
topic: Tetralogy of Fallot Infundibular Spasm and Squatting Physiology
stem: A 3-year-old uncorrected boy with congenital heart disease is brought to the emergency department during an episode of intense crying. His mother reports that he suddenly became acutely dyspneic, agitated, and deeply cyanotic around his mouth and fingers. On physical examination, he instinctively assumes a squatting posture with his knees pressed firmly against his chest. Within 2 minutes of squatting, his cyanosis noticeably diminishes, his breathing slows, and a harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border becomes louder. An echocardiogram previously demonstrated a large malalignment ventricular septal defect, severe infundibular pulmonary stenosis, an overriding aorta, and concentric right ventricular hypertrophy. Which of the following hemodynamic mechanisms explains the rapid clinical improvement produced by squatting in this child?

options.text: Squatting kinks the femoral arteries, increasing systemic vascular resistance and left ventricular afterload, which reverses right-to-left shunting through the VSD
options.explanation: In Tetralogy of Fallot (caused by anterosuperior deviation of the infundibular septum), the magnitude of cyanosis is dictated by the severity of right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) obstruction relative to systemic vascular resistance (SVR). During a hypercyanotic 'tet spell' (triggered by crying, feeding, or agitation), infundibular spasm or a sudden drop in SVR markedly increases RIGHT-TO-LEFT SHUNTING of deoxygenated blood across the large VSD into the systemic circulation, causing profound arterial hypoxemia. When the child SQUATS, two crucial hemodynamic changes occur: (1) Kinking of the femoral arteries and compression of abdominal vessels markedly INCREASES SYSTEMIC VASCULAR RESISTANCE (SVR) and left ventricular afterload. (2) Compression of lower extremity veins transiently increases VENOUS RETURN (preload). The sharp rise in LV pressure exceeds RV systolic pressure, FORCING BLOOD FROM THE RIGHT VENTRICLE ACROSS THE STENOTIC PULMONARY VALVE INTO THE LUNGS instead of through the VSD, restoring pulmonary blood flow, oxygenating arterial blood, and increasing the intensity of the pulmonary stenosis murmur.

options.text: Squatting reduces systemic vascular resistance, decreasing left ventricular afterload and accelerating systemic blood delivery
options.explanation: Decreasing SVR would lower LV pressure below RV pressure, worsening right-to-left shunting and deepening cyanosis; squatting INCREASES SVR.

options.text: Squatting induces sudden vagal bradycardia that terminates a paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
options.explanation: Tet spells are driven by dynamic right-to-left shunting from infundibular spasm, not re-entrant supraventricular tachycardia.

options.text: Squatting elevates intrathoracic pressure, collapsing the inferior vena cava and decreasing right ventricular end-diastolic pressure
options.explanation: Squatting increases venous return (preload) rather than collapsing the IVC; its primary therapeutic benefit is increasing SVR.

options.text: Squatting causes direct mechanical compression of the ventricular septal defect, sealing the intraventricular communication
options.explanation: Squatting cannot mechanically close a congenital fibrous-muscular VSD inside the heart; it alters hemodynamic pressure gradients.

topic: Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome WAS Protein Actin Polymerization Defect
stem: A 14-month-old boy presents with recurrent epistaxis, bloody diarrhea, and persistent severe atopic dermatitis on his face and flexural creases. His past medical history is notable for recurrent otitis media and encapsulated bacterial sinopulmonary infections since 4 months of age. Physical examination reveals widespread petechiae and ecchymoses on his trunk and extremities. Complete blood count shows: hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL, white blood cell count 8,200/microL, and platelet count 24,000/microL. Examination of the peripheral blood smear reveals that the circulating platelets are markedly reduced in number and abnormally small in size (mean platelet volume [MPV] 5.2 fL, normal 7.4-10.4 fL). Serum immunoglobulin profiling demonstrates elevated IgA and IgE, normal IgG, and decreased IgM. Which of the following cellular processes is defective as a result of the mutation in the WAS gene in this patient?

options.text: DNA double-strand break repair via the non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) pathway
options.explanation: Defects in non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) cause ataxia-telangiectasia (ATM mutation) or severe combined immunodeficiency (Artemis/DNA-PKcs mutations), not WAS.

options.text: Actin cytoskeleton remodeling and microfilament nucleation mediated by the Arp2/3 complex in hematopoietic cells
options.explanation: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS) is an X-linked recessive primary immunodeficiency caused by mutations in the WAS gene, which encodes the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASP). WASP is expressed exclusively in hematopoietic cells and acts as an intracellular bridge linking cell surface signaling receptors (via Cdc42 and Rac GTPases) to the actin-related protein 2/3 (Arp2/3) complex. The Arp2/3 complex is essential for NUCLEATING ACTIN POLYMERIZATION and branching of actin microfilaments. Defective WASP disables actin cytoskeleton remodeling, preventing platelet megakaryocyte proplatelet formation (causing MICROTHROMBOCYTOPENIA: small, defective platelets with bleeding), impairing immune synapse formation between T-cells and antigen-presenting cells (causing combined T- and B-cell immunodeficiency with low IgM and high IgA/IgE), and disrupting cell migration, resulting in the classic triad of ECZEMA, MICROTHROMBOCYTOPENIA, and RECURRENT INFECTIONS.

options.text: Integrin-mediated binding of beta-2 integrin (CD18) to intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1)
options.explanation: CD18 deficiency causes Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency type 1 (LAD-1), characterized by absent pus and delayed cord separation with normal-sized platelets.

options.text: Lysosomal acidification and fusion in phagocytes mediated by vesicle-associated membrane proteins
options.explanation: Lysosomal trafficking defects occur in Chédiak-Higashi syndrome (LYST gene), characterized by giant cytoplasmic granules and oculocutaneous albinism.

options.text: Terminal glycosylation of GPI-anchored surface complement regulatory proteins on erythrocyte precursors
options.explanation: GPI anchor failure occurs in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PIGA mutation), causing intravascular hemolysis, not microthrombocytopenia and eczema.

topic: Prader-Willi vs Angelman Syndrome 15q11-q13 Genomic Imprinting
stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric genetics clinic for severe, insatiable hyperphagia, rapid morbid weight gain, and aggressive food-seeking behavior. As an infant, he had severe hypotonia, a weak suck requiring nasogastric tube feeding, and cryptorchidism. Physical examination reveals short stature, small hands and feet, almond-shaped palpebral fissures, a narrow bifrontal diameter, and hypogonadism. Chromosomal microarray analysis reveals a 4-Mb microdeletion on chromosome 15q11.2-q13. Methylation-specific PCR demonstrates that the single remaining allele at this locus is exclusively methylated (maternal pattern) with complete absence of the unmethylated paternal allele. Which of the following genetic mechanisms is the underlying cause of this child's disorder?

options.text: Loss of expression of the maternally inherited UBE3A ubiquitin-protein ligase gene on chromosome 15q11-q13
options.explanation: Loss of the maternal UBE3A allele causes ANGELMAN SYNDROME (severe intellectual disability, seizures, ataxia, inappropriate laughter), not Prader-Willi hyperphagia and obesity.

options.text: Trinucleotide repeat expansion of CTG in the 3' untranslated region of the DMPK gene
options.explanation: DMPK CTG expansion causes Myotonic Dystrophy type 1 (myotonia, muscle wasting, cataracts, testicular atrophy), not Prader-Willi syndrome.

options.text: Loss of expression of paternally inherited genes on chromosome 15q11-q13 (normally silenced on the maternal allele by genomic imprinting)
options.explanation: Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS) and Angelman syndrome (AS) are classic examples of GENOMIC IMPRINTING involving chromosome 15q11-q13. Genomic imprinting is an epigenetic phenomenon in which one parental allele is transcriptionally silenced by DNA methylation during gametogenesis. In normal individuals, genes at the 15q11-q13 locus (including SNRPN, NDN, and snoRNAs) are PATERNALLY EXPRESSED and maternally silenced (imprinted). Conversely, the nearby UBE3A gene is MATERNALLY EXPRESSED in brain neurons and paternally silenced. PRADER-WILLI SYNDROME occurs when there is LOSS OF EXPRESSION OF THE PATERNAL 15q11-q13 ALLELE, most commonly due to a paternal microdeletion (~70%) or maternal uniparental disomy (UPD, ~25%). PWS presents with neonatal hypotonia, failure to thrive, followed in toddlerhood by insatiable hyperphagia, morbid obesity, hypogonadism, and intellectual disability. In contrast, loss of the MATERNAL allele (or paternal UPD) causes ANGELMAN SYNDROME ('happy puppet', inappropriate laughter, seizures, ataxia).

options.text: Paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 11p15.5 leading to overexpression of insulin-like growth factor 2 (IGF-2)
options.explanation: Paternal UPD 11p15.5 causes Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (macrosomia, macroglossia, omphalocele, hemihyperplasia, Wilms tumor), not Prader-Willi syndrome.

options.text: Microdeletion of chromosome 7q11.23 including the elastin gene
options.explanation: 7q11.23 deletion causes Williams syndrome (elfin facies, supravalvular aortic stenosis, hypercalcemia, extreme friendliness), not hyperphagic obesity.

topic: Acetaminophen Hepatotoxicity CYP2E1 NAPQI and N-Acetylcysteine
stem: A 23-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 28 hours after intentionally ingesting 40 tablets of 500-mg acetaminophen during an acute emotional crisis. She initially felt mild nausea that resolved, but over the past 12 hours she developed severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain and persistent vomiting. Physical examination reveals scleral icterus and marked right upper quadrant tenderness with hepatomegaly. Serum chemistries demonstrate: AST 14,800 U/L, ALT 16,200 U/L, total bilirubin 6.8 mg/dL, and prothrombin time 42 seconds (INR 3.8). Which of the following biochemical pathways accounts for the centrilobular hepatic parenchymal necrosis observed in this patient?

options.text: Direct non-enzymatic alkylation of microsomal glucose-6-phosphatase leading to glycogen accumulation and ballooning degeneration
options.explanation: NAPQI binds mitochondrial proteins causing necrotic lysis, not glycogen storage disease from glucose-6-phosphatase inhibition.

options.text: Competitive inhibition of mitochondrial carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1 halting fatty acid beta-oxidation
options.explanation: CPT-1 inhibition causes microvesicular steatosis and hypoketotic hypoglycemia (Reye syndrome or Jamaican vomiting sickness), not fulminant centrilobular transaminitis.

options.text: Irreversible acetylation of canalicular bile salt export pump (BSEP) causing intrahepatic cholestatic hepatitis
options.explanation: BSEP mutations cause progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis (PFIC); APAP causes acute centrilobular necrosis, not pure isolated cholestasis.

options.text: Saturation of glucuronidation and sulfation pathways leading to excessive cytochrome P450 (CYP2E1) conversion to toxic N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI) that depletes glutathione
options.explanation: Acetaminophen (APAP) at therapeutic doses is predominantly metabolized in the liver via Phase II conjugation pathways: GLUCURONIDATION (50-60%) and SULFATION (30-40%) to non-toxic water-soluble metabolites excreted in urine. A small fraction (~5-10%) is oxidized by cytochrome P450 enzymes (predominantly CYP2E1) into the highly reactive, electrophilic, and toxic intermediate N-ACETYL-P-BENZOQUINONE IMINE (NAPQI). Under normal conditions, NAPQI is rapidly detoxified by conjugation with endogenous GLUTATHIONE (GSH) to non-toxic mercapturic acid conjugates. In massive overdose, glucuronidation and sulfation pathways become saturated. Excess APAP is shunted to CYP2E1, producing massive amounts of NAPQI that DEPLETE HEPATIC GLUTATHIONE STORES by > 70-80%. Unconjugated NAPQI covalently binds cysteinyl sulfhydryl groups on hepatic mitochondrial proteins, inducing mitochondrial oxidative stress, opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore, ATP depletion, and massive CENTRILOBULAR (ZONE 3) HEPATOCYTE NECROSIS. Zone 3 is selectively damaged because it has the highest concentration of CYP2E1 and lowest baseline glutathione.

options.text: Immune complex-mediated destruction of portal triad biliary ductules via drug-hapten formation
options.explanation: APAP toxicity is direct, dose-dependent, predictable biochemical necrosis (toxic intrinsic hepatopathy), not an idiosyncratic or immune-mediated drug allergy.

subject: Neurology
topic: Brown-Sequard Syndrome Spinal Cord Hemisection Tract Topography
stem: A 26-year-old man is brought to the trauma center after sustaining a knife stab wound to the middle thoracic back. Neurological examination reveals complete loss of voluntary motor function and spastic weakness in the right lower extremity, accompanied by a right-sided Babinski sign and hyperactive right patellar reflex. Sensory testing demonstrates: (1) Complete loss of vibration sense, light touch, and joint proprioception in the right lower extremity up to the level of the T8 dermatome. (2) Complete loss of pain and temperature sensation in the left lower extremity starting at the T10 dermatome and extending downwards. Pain and temperature sensation on the right side is completely intact below T8. Which of the following spinal cord lesions accounts for this constellation of neurological findings?

options.text: Left-sided spinal cord hemisection at the T10 level
options.explanation: A left-sided hemisection at T10 would produce left-sided motor weakness and left-sided vibration loss, with right-sided pain/temperature loss.

options.text: Complete spinal cord transection at the T8 level
options.explanation: Complete transection produces bilateral loss of motor function and bilateral loss of all sensory modalities below T8.

options.text: Central cord syndrome involving the anterior white commissure from T8 to T10
options.explanation: Central cord syndrome (or syringomyelia) produces bilateral suspended loss of pain/temperature in a cape-like or girdle distribution, sparing dorsal columns.

options.text: Anterior spinal artery thrombosis producing bilateral anterior horn and spinothalamic infarction
options.explanation: Anterior spinal artery syndrome causes bilateral motor paralysis and bilateral loss of pain/temperature with preserved dorsal column vibration/proprioception.

options.text: Right-sided spinal cord hemisection at the T8 level
options.explanation: This patient presents with Brown-Séquard syndrome (spinal cord hemisection), here involving the RIGHT hemicord at the T8 level. The distinctive neuroanatomical pattern arises from the differing decussation levels of the major spinal tracts: (1) LATERAL CORTICOSPINAL TRACT: Upper motor neuron fibers decussate in the medullary pyramids; therefore, a right T8 lesion produces IPSILATERAL (right-sided) spastic paralysis, hyperreflexia, and Babinski sign below the lesion level. (2) DORSAL COLUMN-MEDIAL LEMNISCUS (fasciculus gracilis): First-order sensory axons ascend ipsilaterally in the cord without decussating until the medullary gracile nucleus; therefore, a right T8 lesion produces IPSILATERAL (right-sided) loss of vibration, conscious proprioception, and fine touch below T8. (3) LATERAL SPINOTHALAMIC TRACT: Second-order axons decussate in the anterior white commissure 1 to 2 spinal segments above their entry level; therefore, a right T8 hemisection disrupts ascending crossed fibers that originated from the LEFT side of the body, causing CONTRALATERAL (left-sided) loss of pain and temperature sensation beginning 1 to 2 dermatomes below the lesion (at T10).

stem: A 38-year-old man presents with recurrent renal calculi and persistent epigastric pain. Laboratory studies reveal: serum calcium 11.8 mg/dL, intact parathyroid hormone (PTH) 142 pg/mL (normal 15-65 pg/mL), serum phosphate 2.1 mg/dL, and fasting serum gastrin 890 pg/mL with multiple refractory duodenal ulcers on endoscopy. RET encodes a transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinase for glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF). Activating mutations trigger constitutive, ligand-independent dimerization and kinase signaling, driving medullary thyroid carcinoma (calcitonin-secreting C-cells) and pheochromocytoma.

options.explanation: RET is a proto-oncogene; a single gain-of-function missense mutation in one allele is sufficient to induce oncogenic transformation without loss of heterozygosity.

subject: Genetics
topic: Factor V Leiden Resistance to Activated Protein C Cleavage
stem: A 28-year-old Caucasian woman presents with acute pain and swelling in her left calf 10 days after starting an oral contraceptive pill. Duplex ultrasound confirms an extensive occlusive deep venous thrombosis in the left common femoral and popliteal veins. Her family history is significant for a pulmonary embolism in her mother at age 34 and an unprovoked DVT in her maternal uncle. Coagulation profile shows: PT and PTT within normal limits. In an activated protein C (APC) resistance assay, the patient's PTT fails to prolong normally upon the addition of exogenous activated protein C. Genetic testing confirms a heterozygous missense mutation in the F5 gene (G1691A). Which of the following molecular alterations is responsible for this patient's hereditary thrombophilia?

options.text: Point mutation in the 3' untranslated region (G20210A) of the prothrombin gene causing excessive mRNA translation
options.explanation: Prothrombin G20210A mutation is the second most common inherited thrombophilia; it increases prothrombin mRNA synthesis, not resistance of Factor V to APC cleavage.

options.text: Substitution of glutamine for arginine at position 506 (Arg506Gln) eliminating the primary proteolytic cleavage site for activated Protein C
options.explanation: FACTOR V LEIDEN is the most common inherited cause of venous thromboembolism in Caucasians (~5% carrier frequency). It is caused by a single point mutation in the F5 gene: a guanine-to-adenine substitution at nucleotide 1691 (G1691A), which substitutes GLUTAMINE FOR ARGININE AT CODON 506 (Arg506Gln). In normal hemostasis, Activated Protein C (APC), in complex with its cofactor Protein S, cleaves and inactivates procoagulant Activated Factor V (FVa) at Arg506. The Arg506Gln mutation removes this primary cleavage target, rendering mutated Factor Va resistant to inactivation by APC (ACTIVATED PROTEIN C RESISTANCE). Mutated Factor Va persists in circulation, driving continuous conversion of prothrombin to thrombin by the prothrombinase complex, generating a hypercoagulable state with high risk of recurrent deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, especially when combined with oral contraceptives or pregnancy.

options.text: Nonsense mutation in the antithrombin III gene preventing covalent binding and clearance of thrombin
options.explanation: Antithrombin III deficiency causes severe thrombophilia with heparin resistance, not selective APC resistance at Factor V codon 506.

options.text: Homozygous deletion of the endothelial thrombomodulin receptor halting activation of Protein C
options.explanation: Thrombomodulin binds thrombin to activate Protein C; in Factor V Leiden, Protein C is normally activated, but Factor V cannot be cleaved.

options.text: Autoantibodies directed against phospholipid-bound beta-2-glycoprotein I causing in vitro PTT prolongation
options.explanation: Antiphospholipid syndrome is an acquired autoimmune thrombophilia with lupus anticoagulant (prolonged baseline PTT in vitro), not an inherited Arg506Gln mutation.

subject: Pharmacology
topic: Opioid Withdrawal Adenylate Cyclase Superactivation Rebound
stem: A 31-year-old man with chronic opioid use disorder presents to the emergency department in intense distress 18 hours after his last dose of heroin. He complains of diffuse abdominal cramping, severe muscle aches, diarrhea, and nausea. On physical examination, he is agitated and diaphoresis is noted. Vital signs: blood pressure 152/94 mm Hg, heart rate 118/min, and respirations 22/min. Physical examination demonstrates marked bilateral pupillary dilation (mydriasis), piloerection ('goosebumps'), rhinorrhea, lacrimation, and hyperactive bowel sounds. Which of the following intracellular signaling adaptations directly accounts for the massive autonomic hyperactivity observed during acute opioid withdrawal?

options.text: Permanent inactivation of the vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2) causing vesicular dopamine depletion
options.explanation: VMAT2 inhibition is the mechanism of tetrabenazine and reserpine, causing parkinsonism and depression, not opioid withdrawal hyperactivity.

options.text: Direct block of postsynaptic muscarinic M3 receptors in gastrointestinal smooth muscle
options.explanation: Muscarinic blockade produces constipation and urinary retention, whereas opioid withdrawal causes hyperactive bowel sounds and diarrhea.

options.text: Upregulation and superactivation of adenylate cyclase following abrupt removal of chronic Gi-coupled mu-opioid receptor inhibition
options.explanation: Opioid agonists (heroin, morphine, methadone) bind to Gi-protein-coupled MU-OPIOID RECEPTORS. Gi activation acutely inhibits adenylate cyclase, reduces intracellular cAMP, closes presynaptic N-type voltage-gated calcium channels (inhibiting neurotransmitter release), and opens postsynaptic G-protein-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium (GIRK) channels (hyperpolarizing neurons and suppressing noradrenergic output in the locus coeruleus). With CHRONIC opioid exposure, homeostatic tolerance occurs: neurons upregulate adenylate cyclase, protein kinase A (PKA), and CREB to restore baseline cAMP levels. When the opioid is ABRUPTLY WITHDRAWN, the tonic Gi inhibition is suddenly lifted, unmasking a massive SUPERACTIVATION OF ADENYLATE CYCLASE. This causes runaway intracellular cAMP surges and excessive noradrenergic firing from the locus coeruleus, producing the severe autonomic hyperactivity of withdrawal (tachycardia, hypertension, mydriasis, diaphoresis, diarrhea, piloerection). Clonidine (alpha-2 agonist) relieves withdrawal by restoring Gi-mediated adenylate cyclase inhibition.

options.text: Constitutive opening of gamma-aminobutyric acid type A (GABA-A) chloride channels in the locus coeruleus
options.explanation: GABA-A opening causes central nervous system sedation and depression (the mechanism of benzodiazepines), the opposite of withdrawal hyperactivity.

options.text: Autoantibodies directed against presynaptic alpha-2 adrenergic receptors blocking negative feedback
options.explanation: Opioid withdrawal is an intracellular neuroadaptive signaling phenomenon (cAMP rebound), not an autoimmune receptor disease.

subject: Microbiology
topic: Listeria monocytogenes Actin Rocket Motility and Cell-to-Cell Spread
stem: A 68-year-old renal transplant recipient on chronic immunosuppressive therapy with tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone presents with high fever, headache, photophobia, and altered mental status. Physical examination reveals nuchal rigidity and confusion. Lumbar puncture demonstrates cloudy cerebrospinal fluid with an opening pressure of 260 mm H2O, WBC 1,200/microL with 88% neutrophils, protein 180 mg/dL, and glucose 24 mg/dL. CSF Gram stain reveals intracellular and extracellular Gram-positive coccobacilli. The organism exhibits tumbling motility at 25 C and produces narrow zones of beta-hemolysis on sheep blood agar. Following entry into host macrophages, the bacterium utilizes a surface protein (ActA) to propel itself through the host cytoplasm and directly invade adjacent cells. Which of the following host cytoskeletal proteins is recruited and nucleated by this bacterial factor to achieve intracellular motility?

options.text: Microtubule alpha/beta-tubulin heterodimers polymerizing into dynein-dependent retrograde transport tracks
options.explanation: Microtubules and dynein/kinesin mediate viral retrograde transport (e.g., rabies, herpes simplex), not Listeria actin-based propulsion.

options.text: Keratin intermediate filaments forming stable desmosomal anchoring plaques
options.explanation: Intermediate filaments provide structural tensile strength and do not form dynamic propulsion comet tails.

options.text: Clathrin triskelions assembling into endocytic transport vesicles at the trans-Golgi network
options.explanation: Clathrin coats endocytic vesicles for receptor-mediated endocytosis; it does not generate intracellular motility rockets.

options.text: Host G-actin monomers polymerized into filamentous F-actin comet tails via recruitment of the Arp2/3 complex
options.explanation: Listeria monocytogenes is a facultative intracellular, foodborne Gram-positive rod capable of causing life-threatening meningitis and bacteremia in neonates, pregnant women, and cell-mediated immunocompromised hosts (e.g., organ transplants). After ingestion (unpasteurized dairy, deli meats), Listeria enters host epithelial cells and macrophages via internalins (InlA/InlB). Inside the phagolysosome, it secretes LISTERIOLYSIN O (a pore-forming cytolysin) and phospholipases to escape into the cytosol before lysosomal degradation. In the host cytoplasm, Listeria expresses the surface protein ActA on one bacterial pole. ActA binds and activates the host cell ARP2/3 COMPLEX and neural Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (N-WASP), driving rapid polymerization of host G-ACTIN into FILAMENTOUS F-ACTIN 'COMET TAILS' ('actin rockets'). This actin rocket pushes the bacterium against the host plasma membrane, forming pseudopod-like protrusions (listeriopods) that are engulfed by neighboring cells, allowing cell-to-cell spread WITHOUT entering the extracellular space, completely shielding the pathogen from circulating humoral antibodies.

options.text: Myosin heavy-chain cross-bridges generating sliding filament contractions along microfilaments
options.explanation: Listeria movement is driven purely by the physical force of actin polymerization (monomer addition at the barbed end), not ATP-dependent myosin motor stepping.

subject: Genetics
topic: Duchenne vs Becker Dystrophy Reading Frame Rule and Molecular Pathogenesis
stem: A 4-year-old boy is evaluated for progressive proximal muscle weakness, frequent falling, and difficulty rising from the floor. His mother notes that he places his hands on his thighs and knees to push himself erect (positive Gowers sign). Physical examination shows bilateral pseudohypertrophy of the calf muscles and lumbar hyperlordosis. Serum creatine kinase is markedly elevated at 19,200 U/L. Multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA) of the dystrophin gene (DMD) demonstrates a genomic deletion spanning exons 45 through 50. In contrast, his 32-year-old maternal uncle experiences mild, adult-onset exertional leg cramping but remains ambulatory without assistance. Targeted genetic testing in the uncle reveals a deletion spanning exons 45 through 47 within the same DMD gene. Which of the following molecular mechanisms best accounts for the striking difference in clinical severity between the nephew and his uncle?

options.text: Alternative pre-mRNA splicing with inclusion of a cryptic pseudoexon versus skipped exon silencing by small nuclear ribonucleoproteins
options.explanation: Alternative splicing aberrations and cryptic pseudoexons can alter protein isoform expression, but they do not account for the allelic reading frame difference between Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy.

options.text: Paternal genomic imprinting of the homologous locus versus post-zygotic somatic mosaicism in early myogenic precursor cells
options.explanation: DMD is an X-linked recessive gene subject to maternal transmission, not paternal genomic imprinting; somatic mosaicism explains discordant twin manifestations or carrier females, not the distinct molecular phenotypes of allelic dystrophin deletions.

options.text: Expansion of an unstable non-coding trinucleotide repeat causing transcriptional silencing versus a single missense substitution in the actin-binding domain
options.explanation: Trinucleotide repeat expansions cause disorders such as myotonic dystrophy (CTG repeat in DMPK) and Fragile X syndrome (CGG in FMR1); dystrophinopathy is primarily caused by large intragenic genomic exon deletions.

options.text: Selective degradation of the dystrophin-associated glycoprotein complex by calcium-activated calpain proteases versus intact sarcolemmal linkage
options.explanation: Calpain-3 protease mutations cause autosomal recessive limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2A (calpainopathy), rather than explaining the differential severity of intragenic dystrophin deletions.

options.text: Disruption of the translational reading frame introducing a downstream premature termination codon versus maintenance of the reading frame generating an internally shortened protein
options.explanation: Duchenne (DMD) and Becker (BMD) muscular dystrophies are X-linked recessive allelic disorders caused by mutations in the dystrophin gene (DMD) on Xp21, the largest human gene (79 exons). Dystrophin is an essential structural cytoskeletal protein that anchors intracellular F-actin to the transmembrane dystrophin-glycoprotein complex (specifically beta-dystroglycan), bridging the sarcolemma to the extracellular matrix protein laminin-2. This structural link stabilizes the muscle sarcolemma during the mechanical stress of contraction. The fundamental molecular determinant of disease severity is the READING FRAME RULE: (1) In DUCHENNE muscular dystrophy (nephew with exons 45-50 deletion), the deletion alters the triplet codon reading frame (FRAMESHIFT / OUT-OF-FRAME DELETION). This shifts the translational phase and introduces a PREMATURE STOP CODON downstream. The resulting aberrant mRNA transcript is recognized by the cellular surveillance machinery and undergoes rapid nonsense-mediated decay, resulting in a COMPLETE ABSENCE OF FUNCTIONAL DYSTROPHIN (demonstrated by absent sarcolemmal immunohistochemistry and negative western blot). Contracting myofibers suffer sarcolemmal microtears, unregulated calcium influx, and progressive necrosis with fibrofatty replacement. (2) In BECKER muscular dystrophy (uncle with exons 45-47 deletion), the deletion removes a specific number of nucleotides divisible by three (IN-FRAME DELETION), which preserves the downstream translational triplet reading frame. This produces a truncated, INTERNALLY SHORTENED DYSTROPHIN PROTEIN of reduced molecular weight that retains essential N-terminal actin-binding and C-terminal dystroglycan-binding domains, conferring partial structural stability and a dramatically milder, ambulatory clinical phenotype.
